screens.title: Roles: structure and purpose
screens.narratorSegment: Roles are a directory-based convention in Ansible that group related automation pieces into a single, shareable unit. A role contains tasks, handlers, templates, files, default variables, other variables, metadata, and documentation. This grouping makes it simple to split responsibilities—one role can manage webserver installation while another secures the host. In practice, roles encourage reuse: you can share a webserver role across multiple projects without rewriting tasks. A typical role structure includes defaults for low-precedence settings, handlers for notifications, tasks for the main automation, templates for Jinja2 files, and meta information for dependencies. A common misconception is that roles add complexity; in reality they add predictable structure, which reduces cognitive load when projects grow. For example, calling a role in a playbook is just the roles: list with the role name. This keeps playbooks concise and shifting implementation details back into the role avoids duplication. When you design roles, keep defaults minimal, place host-agnostic content in the role, and reserve inventory or group_vars for environment-specific overrides. A practical test is to extract repeated tasks into a role and confirm the playbook behavior remains identical while the playbook becomes shorter. How might you split an all-in-one playbook into logical roles in your environment?

keyIdea.title: Role best practice
keyIdea.text: Use roles to encapsulate functionality, store defaults, and share automation across projects.

content.html:
Definition

Role directory

my_role/
├── defaults/
├── handlers/
├── tasks/
├── templates/
├── files/
├── vars/
├── meta/
└── README.md
Defaults are low-precedence values you expect to override.
Handlers live in handlers/main.yml and are triggered by notify.
Templates are Jinja2 files placed in templates/ and rendered by the template module.
Example use
Reference a role in a playbook to apply its tasks and handlers to hosts. Ansible will look for tasks/main.yml and handlers/main.yml automatically in the role directory. This keeps the playbook focused on which roles to run and on which hosts.
Playbook snippet
---
- name: Deploy web server with Nginx role
  hosts: webservers
  become: true
  roles:
    - webserver
Concrete example
Extract install and config tasks for Nginx into an nginx_webserver role so different projects can reuse it.
Key takeaway
Roles reduce duplication and make automation easier to reason about.

screens.title: Create a role and defaults
screens.narratorSegment: Start role development by creating the standard directory scaffold so collaborators immediately know where to add content. The ansible-galaxy init command builds this layout. Use defaults/main. yml for settings you expect teams to override, for example nginx_port, nginx_log_path, and app_root_dir. Defaults are lowest precedence, which means they are the safest place to place reasonable values without surprising higher-precedence overrides from inventory or playbook vars. When you initialize a role, inspect keys under defaults and keep secrets out of defaults. Instead, place secrets in encrypted files under vars or vars/secret_vars. yml and manage them with Ansible Vault. A concrete workflow: run ansible-galaxy init roles/nginx_webserver, open defaults/main. yml, and add nginx_port: 8080. Validate by running a dry-run of your playbook to ensure the variables are picked up. A common misconception is that defaults are the same as vars; they are not. vars/main. yml has higher precedence and should be used only for values essential to role behavior. Keep defaults small and document expected overrides in the role README so users know which variables to change. Create a role and defaults means store safe, overridable settings in defaults; reserve vars for fixed role-required values.. In practical terms, initialize role scaffolding and set sensible defaults. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Command
mkdir -p my_nginx_project/roles/nginx_webserver
cd my_nginx_project
ansible-galaxy init roles/nginx_webserver
defaults/main.yml example
nginx_port: 8080
nginx_log_path: /var/log/nginx/custom_access.log
app_root_dir: /var/www/my_app
Run a playbook in check mode to confirm defaults are used correctly. Remember: defaults have the lowest precedence and are intended to be overridden by inventory or -e values.
Concrete example
If you create defaults/main.yml with nginx_port: 8080, a host-specific inventory can override it to 80 without editing the role. This enables environment-specific configuration while keeping the role generic.
Common mistake
Putting secrets in defaults or committing them to VCS. Use Ansible Vault for secrets instead.

screens.title: Jinja2 templating for configs
screens.narratorSegment: Jinja2 templates let you generate configuration files that reflect each host's identity and role defaults. In a template file you embed variables like inventory_hostname and role defaults such as nginx_port. Use filters like default to provide fallbacks when a variable is missing. For example, a typical nginx. conf. j2 uses listen {{ nginx_port | default(80) }} and server_name {{ inventory_hostname }} so each host serves with its assigned name and port. Avoid over-templating: if only a small section needs substitution, prefer line-oriented modules such as lineinfile or blockinfile to keep templates simple and readable. When you deploy templates with the template module, add notify to trigger a handler if the rendered file changes. A common misconception is that templates always complicate testing; instead, test templates by rendering locally or using check mode. Template examples in this lesson include an index. html. j2 that displays inventory_hostname and ansible_os_family. Templating gives you control and reduces duplication because one template can serve many hosts with different values. Jinja2 templating for configs means use jinja2 for meaningful substitutions and prefer targeted file edits for small changes.. In practical terms, render nginx.conf and index.html using variables and facts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Template with intent
keyIdea.text: Use Jinja2 for meaningful substitutions and prefer targeted file edits for small changes.

content.html:
Template: index.html.j2
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>Welcome to {{ inventory_hostname }}</title>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Hello from {{ inventory_hostname }}!</h1>
    <p>This page is served by Nginx on port {{ nginx_port }}.</p>
    <p>OS Family: {{ ansible_os_family }}</p>
</body>
</html>
Template: nginx.conf.j2
server {
    listen {{ nginx_port | default(80) }};
    server_name {{ inventory_hostname }};
    root {{ app_root_dir }};
    index index.html;

    access_log {{ nginx_log_path }};
    error_log /var/log/nginx/custom_error.log;

    location / {
        try_files $uri $uri/ =404;
    }
}
Deploy templates with the template module and include notify to trigger an appropriate handler when the file changes. This keeps service restarts controlled and idempotent.

screens.title: Template deployment and notify
screens.narratorSegment: When you deploy a Jinja2 template, use the ansible. builtin. template module. This module renders the template with the current variable set and writes the resulting file to the remote host. If the rendered content differs from the remote file, the task reports changed, and you can attach notify: restart nginx to that task. Notify signals an idempotent handler defined in handlers/main. yml. Handlers run once per play at the end, even if multiple tasks notify the same handler. This prevents repeated restarts during a single run. For example, if multiple templates change that all need nginx restarted, the handler will restart nginx only once. A common pitfall is placing service restarts directly after a task; that causes restarts even when no change occurred. Another safety practice is to ensure the handler itself is idempotent and tolerates being called in any state. Define handlers using ansible. builtin. service with state: restarted. Finally, test notify behavior by running the playbook twice: the first run should change files and notify the handler; the second run should report no changes and not restart the service.

keyIdea.title: Controlled restarts
keyIdea.text: Use notify and handlers so services restart only when something actually changed.

content.html:
Task with notify
- name: Deploy custom Nginx configuration
  ansible.builtin.template:
    src: nginx.conf.j2
    dest: /etc/nginx/sites-available/default
    owner: root
    group: root
    mode: '0644'
  notify: restart nginx
If the template changes, the task reports changed and the handler will be queued. Handlers run at the end of the play and only once per handler name.
Handler example
---
- name: restart nginx
  ansible.builtin.service:
    name: nginx
    state: restarted
  become: true
Pro tip
Test handlers by running the playbook twice and confirming only the first run triggers the restart.
Common mistake
Avoid direct immediate restarts in tasks; they cause unnecessary disruptions when no change occurred.

screens.title: Ansible Vault fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: Ansible Vault encrypts files or variable content so sensitive data is not stored in plain text. Use ansible-vault create to generate encrypted files and ansible-vault edit to modify them. When a playbook needs those secrets, include the file with include_vars and then reference the values in templates or tasks. For example, create roles/nginx_webserver/vars/secret_vars. yml and encrypt it with ansible-vault create. In your tasks, include_vars file: secret_vars. yml name: secrets and then reference {{ secrets. db_password }} in templates. Do not commit unencrypted secrets to version control. Vault passwords can be provided at runtime with --ask-vault-pass or via a vault_password_file that has restricted permissions. A misconception is that vault complicates automation; in practice, using a properly secured password file and limited access keeps automation both secure and automatable. Also remember to avoid placing the vault password in shared repositories. Finally, test by running the playbook with and without the vault password to observe failures when secrets are unavailable. Ansible Vault fundamentals means use ansible vault for any secret and include encrypted files with include_vars to reference their values safely.. In practical terms, protect secrets and use include_vars to load encrypted files. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Vault commands
ansible-vault create roles/nginx_webserver/vars/secret_vars.yml
ansible-vault edit roles/nginx_webserver/vars/secret_vars.yml
ansible-vault view roles/nginx_webserver/vars/secret_vars.yml
Store API keys, passwords, and other sensitive values in Vault-encrypted files. Provide the password at runtime rather than embedding it in scripts or code repositories.
Include and use
- name: Load secret variables
  ansible.builtin.include_vars:
    file: secret_vars.yml
    name: secrets

# then use {{ secrets.db_password }} in templates or tasks
Security note
Use a vault password file with strict permissions for automation, and never commit that file to VCS.

screens.title: Facts and variable precedence
screens.narratorSegment: Ansible gathers facts about managed nodes, such as operating system family, IP addresses, memory, and more. These facts become variables like ansible_os_family and ansible_default_ipv4. address and are available to playbooks and templates. In addition to facts, Ansible supports variables at multiple levels: inventory, playbook, role defaults, role vars, and extra variables passed on the command line. Each level has a defined precedence. The important rule is that higher-precedence variables override lower-precedence ones. For example, extra variables passed with -e take precedence over playbook variables and defaults. Defaults placed in roles are the lowest priority and intentionally designed to be overridden. A common mistake is expecting defaults to be immutable; instead, they are intentionally flexible. For large environments, gathering facts on every run can be slow; configure fact caching to improve performance. When troubleshooting unexpected values, inspect variable precedence by running a play with -vvv or using debug statements to print variable values. Understanding precedence avoids surprising overrides in production automation. Facts and variable precedence means remember that extra vars override inventory and defaults. use the right level to control scope and intent.. In practical terms, how ansible determines which variables win. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Common facts
  • ansible_os_family — OS family such as Debian or RedHat
  • ansible_default_ipv4.address — default IPv4 address
  • ansible_memtotal_mb — memory in MB
Use facts in templates and conditions to make decisions like which package name to install or which path to use for logs.
Variable precedence (simplified)
Extra vars (-e) > Playbook vars > Inventory vars > Role vars > Role defaults. When debugging, print values with debug to confirm which level provided the final value.
Tip

screens.title: Common mistakes & mitigations
screens.narratorSegment: Advanced playbooks are powerful but can produce subtle failures if you fall into common traps. First, over-templating: templating an entire file when only a single value needs substitution increases complexity and makes diffs noisy. Mitigation: use lineinfile or blockinfile for small changes. Second, vault password management: storing the vault password in an insecure file or repository defeats Vault's purpose. Mitigation: use a restricted permission vault_password_file or a secrets manager integration. Third, handler idempotence: handlers must be safe to run even when repeatedly queued; ensure the handler behaves idempotently. Fourth, fact gathering overhead: gathering facts on every run for large inventories is slow. Mitigate with fact caching, selecting specific facts or disabling fact gathering when unnecessary. Fifth, role dependencies: declaring dependencies in meta/main. yml can introduce ordering effects; document and test dependencies to avoid surprises. Each common mistake is paired with a mitigation so your automation remains robust and predictable in production. screens.title: Role dependencies and meta
screens.narratorSegment: Roles can depend on other roles. Use meta/main. yml to declare those dependencies so Ansible executes them in the correct order. A typical use is a webserver role that depends on a common security_hardening role. Declaring dependencies creates predictable execution order without having to list all roles manually in the playbook. However, dependencies introduce coupling. Keep them minimal and document why they exist. Another pattern is to have a meta role that aggregates related roles for a full stack deployment. When testing, run roles individually and also run the aggregate play to ensure ordering and variable exposure are correct. screens.title: Assessment: conditional restarts and secure variables
screens.narratorSegment: Assessment exercises help confirm your understanding. One common scenario asks: restart a service only when its configuration file changes. The idiomatic solution is to define a handler named restart my_app_service in handlers/main. yml and add notify: restart my_app_service to the task that modifies the configuration. This approach ensures the restart runs only when the task reports changed. Avoid placing a direct service restart task after the configuration task because that restarts the service on every run. Another question asks how to store a database password for a template. The correct approach is to encrypt the password with ansible-vault in a file such as vars/secrets. yml, include it with include_vars, and reference the secret in your Jinja2 template. This keeps secrets out of plain text repositories and allows automated runs by supplying the vault password at runtime. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how to design Ansible playbooks that scale and remain maintainable as your infrastructure grows. We focus on roles to structure content, Jinja2 templates to generate configuration dynamically, handlers to control service restarts, Ansible Vault to protect secrets, and facts and variable precedence to control behavior across environments. You will see a concrete example of a reusable nginx_webserver role that installs Nginx, deploys templated files, and restarts the service only when needed. I will also explain common mistakes like over-templating and insecure vault handling, and show safe practices such as using default role variables and include_vars to load encrypted secrets. By the end you should know how to organize role directories, call roles from a playbook, embed variables into templates, notify handlers, and reference vault-encrypted data. This foundation helps you deliver reproducible deployments that are easier to test and share across teams. Consider how these patterns reduce duplication and where you might apply them in your environments.

By the end of this chapter you will organize playbooks using roles so your automation is modular and shareable across projects. You will author Jinja2 templates that generate configuration files using inventory variables and facts, making host-specific configuration deterministic. You will manage secrets using Ansible Vault, learning commands to create, edit, and include encrypted variable files safely. You will implement handlers and notify statements so services restart only when configuration changes, preserving uptime and avoiding unnecessary restarts. You will also leverage Ansible facts and variable precedence so your playbooks behave predictably across inventories. Each objective is paired with a practical milestone that demonstrates competence: a working nginx_webserver role, templated configuration files that read facts, an encrypted variable file loaded with include_vars, handlers that execute only when notified, and a short test showing variable override precedence. These skills reduce risk in production automation and make collaboration across teams easier.

This objective set ties directly to the hands-on nginx_webserver role you will build. First, initialize the role structure so you understand where tasks, handlers, templates, defaults, and vars belong. Second, write templates that use inventory_hostname and role defaults so the same template renders differently per host without changing the code. Third, encrypt a small variable file with Ansible Vault and include it with include_vars to confirm the vault file loads at runtime. Fourth, wire a template task to notify a handler so the service restarts only when the file has actually changed. Each milestone is practical and testable: run ansible-playbook against a managed node and verify files, service state, and logs. These outcomes ensure you can replicate the pattern across other roles and teams, and that your automation remains auditable and secure.

Roles are a directory-based convention in Ansible that group related automation pieces into a single, shareable unit. A role contains tasks, handlers, templates, files, default variables, other variables, metadata, and documentation. This grouping makes it simple to split responsibilities—one role can manage webserver installation while another secures the host. In practice, roles encourage reuse: you can share a webserver role across multiple projects without rewriting tasks. A typical role structure includes defaults for low-precedence settings, handlers for notifications, tasks for the main automation, templates for Jinja2 files, and meta information for dependencies. A common misconception is that roles add complexity; in reality they add predictable structure, which reduces cognitive load when projects grow. For example, calling a role in a playbook is just the roles: list with the role name. This keeps playbooks concise and shifting implementation details back into the role avoids duplication. When you design roles, keep defaults minimal, place host-agnostic content in the role, and reserve inventory or group_vars for environment-specific overrides. A practical test is to extract repeated tasks into a role and confirm the playbook behavior remains identical while the playbook becomes shorter. How might you split an all-in-one playbook into logical roles in your environment?

Start role development by creating the standard directory scaffold so collaborators immediately know where to add content. The ansible-galaxy init command builds this layout. Use defaults/main. yml for settings you expect teams to override, for example nginx_port, nginx_log_path, and app_root_dir. Defaults are lowest precedence, which means they are the safest place to place reasonable values without surprising higher-precedence overrides from inventory or playbook vars. When you initialize a role, inspect keys under defaults and keep secrets out of defaults. Instead, place secrets in encrypted files under vars or vars/secret_vars. yml and manage them with Ansible Vault. A concrete workflow: run ansible-galaxy init roles/nginx_webserver, open defaults/main. yml, and add nginx_port: 8080. Validate by running a dry-run of your playbook to ensure the variables are picked up. A common misconception is that defaults are the same as vars; they are not. vars/main. yml has higher precedence and should be used only for values essential to role behavior. Keep defaults small and document expected overrides in the role README so users know which variables to change. Create a role and defaults means store safe, overridable settings in defaults; reserve vars for fixed role-required values.. In practical terms, initialize role scaffolding and set sensible defaults. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Jinja2 templates let you generate configuration files that reflect each host's identity and role defaults. In a template file you embed variables like inventory_hostname and role defaults such as nginx_port. Use filters like default to provide fallbacks when a variable is missing. For example, a typical nginx. conf. j2 uses listen {{ nginx_port | default(80) }} and server_name {{ inventory_hostname }} so each host serves with its assigned name and port. Avoid over-templating: if only a small section needs substitution, prefer line-oriented modules such as lineinfile or blockinfile to keep templates simple and readable. When you deploy templates with the template module, add notify to trigger a handler if the rendered file changes. A common misconception is that templates always complicate testing; instead, test templates by rendering locally or using check mode. Template examples in this lesson include an index. html. j2 that displays inventory_hostname and ansible_os_family. Templating gives you control and reduces duplication because one template can serve many hosts with different values. Jinja2 templating for configs means use jinja2 for meaningful substitutions and prefer targeted file edits for small changes.. In practical terms, render nginx.conf and index.html using variables and facts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When you deploy a Jinja2 template, use the ansible. builtin. template module. This module renders the template with the current variable set and writes the resulting file to the remote host. If the rendered content differs from the remote file, the task reports changed, and you can attach notify: restart nginx to that task. Notify signals an idempotent handler defined in handlers/main. yml. Handlers run once per play at the end, even if multiple tasks notify the same handler. This prevents repeated restarts during a single run. For example, if multiple templates change that all need nginx restarted, the handler will restart nginx only once. A common pitfall is placing service restarts directly after a task; that causes restarts even when no change occurred. Another safety practice is to ensure the handler itself is idempotent and tolerates being called in any state. Define handlers using ansible. builtin. service with state: restarted. Finally, test notify behavior by running the playbook twice: the first run should change files and notify the handler; the second run should report no changes and not restart the service.

Ansible Vault encrypts files or variable content so sensitive data is not stored in plain text. Use ansible-vault create to generate encrypted files and ansible-vault edit to modify them. When a playbook needs those secrets, include the file with include_vars and then reference the values in templates or tasks. For example, create roles/nginx_webserver/vars/secret_vars. yml and encrypt it with ansible-vault create. In your tasks, include_vars file: secret_vars. yml name: secrets and then reference {{ secrets. db_password }} in templates. Do not commit unencrypted secrets to version control. Vault passwords can be provided at runtime with --ask-vault-pass or via a vault_password_file that has restricted permissions. A misconception is that vault complicates automation; in practice, using a properly secured password file and limited access keeps automation both secure and automatable. Also remember to avoid placing the vault password in shared repositories. Finally, test by running the playbook with and without the vault password to observe failures when secrets are unavailable. Ansible Vault fundamentals means use ansible vault for any secret and include encrypted files with include_vars to reference their values safely.. In practical terms, protect secrets and use include_vars to load encrypted files. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Ansible gathers facts about managed nodes, such as operating system family, IP addresses, memory, and more. These facts become variables like ansible_os_family and ansible_default_ipv4. address and are available to playbooks and templates. In addition to facts, Ansible supports variables at multiple levels: inventory, playbook, role defaults, role vars, and extra variables passed on the command line. Each level has a defined precedence. The important rule is that higher-precedence variables override lower-precedence ones. For example, extra variables passed with -e take precedence over playbook variables and defaults. Defaults placed in roles are the lowest priority and intentionally designed to be overridden. A common mistake is expecting defaults to be immutable; instead, they are intentionally flexible. For large environments, gathering facts on every run can be slow; configure fact caching to improve performance. When troubleshooting unexpected values, inspect variable precedence by running a play with -vvv or using debug statements to print variable values. Understanding precedence avoids surprising overrides in production automation. Facts and variable precedence means remember that extra vars override inventory and defaults. use the right level to control scope and intent.. Advanced playbooks are powerful but can produce subtle failures if you fall into common traps. First, over-templating: templating an entire file when only a single value needs substitution increases complexity and makes diffs noisy. Mitigation: use lineinfile or blockinfile for small changes. Second, vault password management: storing the vault password in an insecure file or repository defeats Vault's purpose. Mitigation: use a restricted permission vault_password_file or a secrets manager integration. Third, handler idempotence: handlers must be safe to run even when repeatedly queued; ensure the handler behaves idempotently. Fourth, fact gathering overhead: gathering facts on every run for large inventories is slow. Mitigate with fact caching, selecting specific facts or disabling fact gathering when unnecessary. Fifth, role dependencies: declaring dependencies in meta/main. yml can introduce ordering effects; document and test dependencies to avoid surprises. Roles can depend on other roles. Use meta/main. yml to declare those dependencies so Ansible executes them in the correct order. A typical use is a webserver role that depends on a common security_hardening role. Declaring dependencies creates predictable execution order without having to list all roles manually in the playbook. However, dependencies introduce coupling. Keep them minimal and document why they exist. Another pattern is to have a meta role that aggregates related roles for a full stack deployment. A misconception is that dependencies remove the need for clear documentation; they do not. Always record expected variable contracts in role README files so dependent roles understand which variables to set or override. When testing, run roles individually and also run the aggregate play to ensure ordering and variable exposure are correct. Assessment exercises help confirm your understanding. One common scenario asks: restart a service only when its configuration file changes. The idiomatic solution is to define a handler named restart my_app_service in handlers/main. yml and add notify: restart my_app_service to the task that modifies the configuration. This approach ensures the restart runs only when the task reports changed. Avoid placing a direct service restart task after the configuration task because that restarts the service on every run. This keeps secrets out of plain text repositories and allows automated runs by supplying the vault password at runtime. Remember three core ideas as you design advanced playbooks. First, roles encapsulate related automation into reusable units that contain tasks, handlers, templates, defaults, vars, and meta. Second, Jinja2 templates combined with the template module let you render configuration files using variables and facts, and you should connect template tasks to handlers so services restart only when content changes. Third, Ansible Vault protects sensitive data; encrypt secrets and include them with include_vars so templates and tasks can reference them safely. Keep defaults minimal, understand variable precedence, and avoid over-templating. These practices help your automation remain maintainable, secure, and predictable as your infrastructure scales.
